details:
**The Twelve Labors for King Eurystheus**
After Hera drove Heracles mad and he killed his first wife Megara and their children, he served his cousin Eurystheus, king of Tiryns, as penance by performing twelve labors. Eurystheus was so frightened of Heracles and the creatures he brought back that he hid in a bronze wine jar (pithos). He also refused to count two labors, the Hydra (because Iolaus helped) and the Augean stables (because Heracles asked Augeas for payment), so ten tasks grew to twelve.

**Nemean Lion**
The first labor. The lion's hide could not be pierced by arrows, so Heracles strangled it with his bare hands. He then wore its skin as his trademark cloak, and that lion pelt and his club are his standard attributes.

**Lernaean Hydra and Iolaus**
The second labor was to kill the many-headed serpent of Lerna, which grew back two heads for each one cut off. Heracles drove it from its lair at the spring of Amymone with flaming arrows, and his nephew and charioteer Iolaus burned (cauterized) each neck stump with a torch so the heads could not regrow. Hera sent a giant crab that pinched Heracles's foot during the fight. Heracles dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisonous blood and buried its immortal head under a rock.

**Deianira, Nessus, and the poisoned shirt**
Heracles won his second wife Deianira by wrestling the river god Achelous and breaking off one of his horns. When the centaur Nessus tried to carry her off, Heracles shot him with a Hydra-poisoned arrow. The dying Nessus told Deianira that his blood was a love charm. Years later, jealous of Heracles's captive Iole, she soaked a shirt (tunic) in it and sent it to him with the herald Lichas. The poison burned Heracles's flesh, he hurled Lichas into the sea, and he had himself burned alive on a pyre on Mount Oeta. He then rose to Olympus as a god and married Hebe, goddess of youth.

**Augean stables**
For one labor Heracles had to clean the enormous, filthy cattle stables of King Augeas of Elis in a single day. He did it by diverting the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them. When Augeas refused to pay the promised tenth of his cattle, Heracles later deposed him and put his son Phyleus on the throne.

**Birth from Alcmene, Amphitryon, and Iphicles**
Zeus took the form of Amphitryon to sleep with his wife Alcmene, so Heracles was born alongside his mortal twin half-brother Iphicles, Amphitryon's son. Hera had the birth goddess Eileithyia delay Heracles's birth so that Eurystheus would be born first and inherit power. Alcmene's servant Galanthis tricked Eileithyia into ending the delay and was turned into a weasel. Heracles's birth name was Alcaeus (or Alcides).

**Strangling the snakes in the cradle**
As an infant, Heracles strangled two serpents that Hera sent to kill him, while his twin Iphicles screamed in terror. This is the first proof of his superhuman strength.

**Serving Queen Omphale**
After throwing Iphitus, son of King Eurytus, from the walls of Tiryns, Heracles was told by an oracle (the priestess Xenoclea) that he could be purified only by being sold into slavery. He served Queen Omphale of Lydia, often described as wearing women's clothes and doing spinning while she wore his lion skin. During this period he also captured the Cercopes, mischievous thieves whom he hung upside down from a pole on his shoulder and then released because their jokes amused him.

**Stymphalian Birds and the krotala**
Another labor was to drive off the metal-feathered, man-eating birds of Lake Stymphalia. Athena gave Heracles bronze krotala (rattles or castanets made by Hephaestus), and their noise scared the birds into the air so he could shoot them.

**Bow and poisoned arrows, given to Philoctetes**
Heracles's arrows, dipped in the Hydra's blood, killed Nessus, the Stymphalian birds, and Geryon. Because Philoctetes lit Heracles's funeral pyre, he received the bow and arrows. The seer Helenus later prophesied that the Greeks needed these weapons to take Troy, so they fetched Philoctetes from Lemnos, where he had been left with a festering snake bite.

**Cattle of Geryon and the cup of Helios**
For the tenth labor Heracles fetched the cattle of the three-bodied giant Geryon from the far west, killing the two-headed dog Orthrus and the herdsman Eurytion. When the sun's heat bothered him, he aimed an arrow at Helios, who admired his boldness and lent him his golden cup (boat) to sail across the ocean.

**Capture of Cerberus**
The twelfth and final labor was to bring the three-headed hound of Hades up from the underworld. Heracles wrestled the dog into submission with his bare hands. While in the underworld he freed Theseus and lifted the boulder pinning Ascalaphus.

**Hylas and the Argonauts**
Heracles sailed with the Argonauts, accompanied by his beloved young companion Hylas, son of the Dryopian king Theiodamas, whom Heracles had killed. When Hylas was pulled into a spring by water nymphs in Mysia, Heracles stayed behind searching for him and the Argo left without him.

**Linus and Chiron**
As a youth Heracles killed his music teacher Linus (who also taught Orpheus) by striking him with a lyre after being scolded. He also accidentally wounded the wise centaur Chiron with a poisoned arrow while fighting centaurs, a related story to the one in which his poisoned arrows killed the centaur Pholus during the hunt for the Erymanthian Boar.

**Wrestling Antaeus and Thanatos**
Heracles defeated the Libyan giant Antaeus, a son of Poseidon and Gaia who drew strength from touching the earth, by lifting him off the ground and crushing him. He also wrestled Thanatos (Death) to bring Alcestis back to her husband Admetus. Other popular side adventures include killing the Egyptian king Busiris, who sacrificed strangers, and his first sack of Troy after King Laomedon refused him the promised horses, sparing only Priam (Podarces), who was ransomed by his sister Hesione.
